body.en: The levels sit on the map in chapters, and each chapter answers one question. Pass a level and the levels after it open; where the path splits, take the branches in any order, and pass them all to go on.
If you would rather not go in order, turn on “Unlock all”: any level can be played straight away, and your progress is still recorded. The map also has your Parts and this Encyclopedia.

title.en: Intro, goal and how to play

body.en: The first time you enter a level, a few pages of Intro open first, explaining the level’s new problem and anything new in it. To read them again, click “Intro” in the top bar; on a computer, ← and → turn the pages.
In the level’s brief, the Goal says what the level wants worked out, and How to play says what you have to do. When you are stuck, read the goal again first.
Some levels come in several stages, asking a few questions in a row about the same map; some stages hand their circuit board on to the next.
Not every level needs a circuit: in some you draw arrows, fill in numbers or trace routes on the board by hand, and “How to play” says which.
To begin with you have just two things: cells and arrows. A cell holds a number; an arrow carries the number in the cell it starts from into the cell it ends at.
When several arrows point at the same cell, the cell adds up everything it receives; a cell no arrow points at holds 0.

To draw an arrow, click one cell and then another; connect the same two cells again and the arrow is removed. A cell can only be worked out once every arrow pointing at it has delivered, so arrows must never loop round.
In circuit-board levels the computing is done by a robot. It walks the whole table cell by cell, runs the same circuit board on every cell, and writes the result into the cell it stands on.

The red frame in the middle of the robot’s view is the cell it stands on. For the circuit board to read a cell in view, click it in the view: the “View” part on the left of the circuit board gains an output that reads it, and a cell being read has a blue frame in the view. Cells beyond the table show “out”, and what they send is “—”.
The This cell panel under the view lists facts about the cell. Click one, and the “This cell” part gains an output that reads it.

A circuit board is the rule for one cell: you write it once, and the robot follows it on every cell. The “View” and “This cell” parts are its inputs, the red-framed “this cell” is its output, and components go in between.

A wire always runs from an output dot to an input dot: drag from one dot to the other, or click one dot and then the other. An input takes one wire, so a new one replaces the old; an output can feed several inputs.

A wire that cannot go in is refused, with the reason: the signals do not match, say, or the wire would make a loop. On a computer, click a part or a wire to select it and press Delete to remove it; drag the empty background to move the board around.
On a phone, the board has a wire display button that switches between “All wires”, “No input wires” and “No wires”, so a busy board is easier to read.

Before a run, the test board is a place to try things out: click a cell to type a number into it, or to send the robot there, and the red frame shows the circuit board’s answer for that cell straight away. On a computer you can type the digits, press Enter to confirm and Esc to put the keypad away.

Click Run tests and the board is cleared; the robot starts again and walks it in the scan order, one test after another. If a test fails, the robot stops on the cell that went wrong: the numbers in the view and on the circuit board are what it saw and worked out there.

After a run, click any computed cell to see what the machine worked out there, and click again to leave it; “Back to the test board” takes you back to trying things out. Some levels only check the answer cell and some check the whole table; “How to play” says which.

Components are little machines on the circuit board: they take signals at their input dots and send a result from their output dot. On a computer, click one in the Parts window to put it on the board; on a phone, tap one in the tray or hold and drag it onto a slot, and drag it back to the tray to remove it. Click a placed component to change its settings.
A signal can be a number, or “—”, which means “there is no road here”, or simply nothing. An input with no wire reads “—”.
A <part-ref to="part:msum"></part-ref> adds up the numbers wired into it; it skips “—”, and only outputs “—” when every input is “—”.
After some levels, the circuit board you built becomes a part: a new component in the tray. Put it on the board and wire it up, and it works without being built again.
The names on a part’s inputs only say how it was first used. A part cares about structure, not names: whatever you wire into it is what it works on.
Your Parts, on the map, keep every part you have collected along the way.
Each level decides which robot model it uses. The first time a new model turns up, the Intro introduces it.

The biggest difference between models is their vision. Boxy sees the ring of cells around it, 3×3; Farsight sees two rings, 5×5. A circuit board can only read cells in view, so reading further takes a different model.
Longarm has a telescopic arm: how far it reaches depends on the cell’s own data, such as reaching left by as many cells as “this item’s weight”, so it can read cells outside its view.
Under the view is the arm’s own row, showing the cells it can reach; click one, and the “View” part gains an output that reads it.

In levels that keep a single row and rewrite it in place, the machine rewrites that row in one rewrite direction: right to left when each item can be taken at most once, left to right when each can be taken many times.

During a run, yellow marks the cell being rewritten, and red means a cell read a value that was rewritten earlier in the same pass. The direction decides whether a cell reads an old value or a new one, and so what the row means.
Broom has a sweep arm: it sweeps a whole run of cells in one go and feeds every number in the run into the circuit board, however many cells the run has.
A wire carrying a whole segment is drawn thicker. Mergers, Adders and Multipliers take a whole segment directly, and every number in it takes part; gates do not take segments.
The robot walks the table in a scan order: row by row from the top left, row by row from the bottom right… Each level’s introduction tells you how it walks.
The order has to follow the circuit: a cell that is read must come before the cell that reads it. A circuit that reads right and down has to start from the bottom right.
In some levels the table is stacked in several layers: besides “which cell”, the state remembers other things too, such as which keys are in hand. Every extra thing remembered doubles the layers.
Layercake works once on the same cell of every layer, and every layer shares the same circuit board; the This cell panel tells it how things stand on that layer.
Remember too little and the answers go wrong; remember too much and the table explodes. A good state is just enough: it remembers only what affects the future.

Think of each cell as a small question and each arrow as “this question needs that answer”, and you have a dependency graph. The cell an arrow starts from must always be worked out before the cell it ends at.

The graph must have no loops: if A waits for B while B waits for A, neither can ever be worked out. A graph whose arrows have a direction and never loop round is called a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
Behind a table there is a graph like this too: each cell is a state, and arrows point into it from the cells it reads. That is the “state graph” in the game’s name.
Dynamic programming is a way of solving problems: break a big problem into small ones, solve the small ones first and write their answers in a table, then build the big answer out of them.

The small problems are called subproblems. “How many routes lead to school?” breaks down into “how many routes lead to each stop just before school?”, and those break down again, all the way back to the start.
The name sounds grand, but the doing is just filling in a table: each cell is worked out once, written down, and simply looked up by the cells that come after it.
The rule for working out a cell from other cells is called the transition; written as a formula it is a recurrence, such as “this crossing = up + left”.

The trusty way to find the rule is to look only at the last step: just before arriving here, where could the last step have come from? Each possibility matches a cell that has already been worked out, and you combine them.
In the game, the circuit board is the transition: written once, and followed by the robot on every cell.

A rule has to start somewhere. Small problems that need no further breaking down, like the start, have answers that are simply given; these are the base cases. Standing at the start, for instance, counts as 1 route.
Along the edges of the table, some ways in fall outside it; there is no road there, and that shows as “—”. The rule has to cope with these “—”s, or the edge cells come out wrong.
Get a base case wrong and every cell after it goes wrong too. When a test fails, look at the start and the edge cells first.
The same skeleton answers different questions. To ask how many, add up all the ways in; to ask what is best, pick the best of the ways in, then count in this cell’s own cost.
On the circuit board, the difference is often just the Merger’s operation: “sum” counts, “min” finds the fewest, “max” finds the most.
Optimising can be broken down like this because every stretch of a best route is itself the best way to reach the end of that stretch. This is called optimal substructure.
The table tells you what the best result is, but not straight out how to get it. Yet every cell’s number came from one of its ways in: the table has also kept every choice.

Start at the end and ask “which way in did this cell’s number come from?”, step back to that cell, and ask again, all the way back to the start: you have recovered the whole route. Working backwards like this is called backtracking.

Ask your way down: to know how many ways lead to step n, ask step n − 1 and step n − 2, which ask further down in turn… and the same small question gets asked again and again. These are overlapping subproblems.
The fix is simple: write down every answer you work out, and next time just look it up instead of working it out again. That is why filling the table computes each cell only once.
With the asking method, every extra step multiplies the number of questions by a fixed factor. Growth that snowballs like this is exponential: add a few more steps and the asking never finishes.
Filling the table takes about as many computations as the table has cells: one more step is just one more cell. Growth like n or n² as the problem gets bigger is called polynomial time.
Dynamic programming is fast not because any one step is clever, but because nothing is repeated: an exponential number of routes is squeezed into a polynomial number of cells.
The situation a cell of the table stands for is called a state, such as “standing at this crossing” or “having seen the first few houses”. The number in the cell is that state’s answer.
A good state remembers everything that affects the future. If two different histories land in the same cell but can go on to do different things, that cell cannot keep an accurate answer.
Designing the state is the hardest and most important step in dynamic programming: only once you know what each cell holds can you write its rule.
If the state forgets something, make it remember one more thing: copy the table into several layers, one per situation. This is called adding a dimension to the state.
Then lay down how to move between layers. A set of situations plus the rules for switching between them is called a state machine.
To prove a state design falls short, you only need one counterexample: two histories that land in the same state but have different futures.
A counterexample does more than show something is wrong; it points to the fix: whatever the two histories differ in is what the state should also remember.

The machine computes once per cell, however many cells the table has. Multiply the sizes of the state’s dimensions and you get the number of cells: two words, for instance, give an alignment table of roughly one length times the other cells.

Each extra yes-or-no thing remembered doubles the layers: remember k things and there are 2 to the power k layers. Remembering more feels safer, but the table keeps growing; this is called state explosion.
So a good state is just enough: it leaves out nothing that affects the future, and remembers nothing that does not.

Real problems never say on them. Faced with a new one, start with three questions: how many possibilities are there for the last step? Can the answers to small problems build the big one? What must the state remember?
Some problems do not need it at all: if there are no smaller problems to break off and build back up, simply looking through from start to finish is enough.

The machine works through the cells in some computing order. The cells a cell reads must be ready first, so a legal order has just one requirement: every cell comes after the cells it reads. An order that meets it is called a topological order.
The order and the circuit go together: the circuit decides which cells each cell reads, and so which orders are legal; change the order, and the cells the circuit can read change with it.
Settling an order first and filling in cell by cell, from small problems up to the big one, is called bottom-up. Every table up to this point was filled in that way.

The other way round, starting from the big question and asking whichever cells it needs, is called top-down; in a program it is recursion. It needs no order worked out in advance, but unless the answers are written down, the same question gets asked many times.
Ask top-down, but write down every answer you get and look it up the next time it is asked: this is called memoisation, or memoised recursion. That way each cell is really worked out only once.
Bottom-up filling and memoised recursion walk the same dependency graph, just in different ways: one settles the order and then fills in, the other works things out as it asks.

When the arrows loop round, no order can promise that everything read is already computed. The answer is to scan in rounds: cells not reached yet read “—” or what the last round left, and every round brings the answers a step closer to the truth. During a run, yellow frames mark the cells that changed this round.

When a round changes nothing, it stops: every cell now satisfies its own rule, which is called a fixed point, and repeating until nothing changes is called iterating to convergence. If the rule keeps making the numbers bigger and never settles, the machine tells you the table never settles.
Improving shortest-route answers round after round like this is the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Routers on a network swapping notes on “how far it is to everywhere” work the same way.
Climbing 1 or 2 steps at a time, how many ways are there to reach step n? It is the most common first problem in dynamic programming.

On the surface it has nothing to do with counting routes. But look only at the last step and a familiar structure appears: each cell’s answer comes from a few earlier cells, plus a start. Spot the same structure and an old part can be used as it is.
A string of letters that appears in order in both of two strings, with letters skipped in between allowed, is a common subsequence. The longest one is the longest common subsequence.
Finding what changed between two files, comparing how alike two stretches of DNA are, telling whether one piece of homework was copied from another: they all use it.
Changing one word into another, deleting, inserting or replacing one letter per step, what is the fewest number of steps? That number is the edit distance.

It uses the alignment table too. Each of a cell’s ways in stands for one kind of change, and each carries its own cost; pick the cheapest. The same table with a different circuit board answers a different question.
Spelling correction and the search box’s “did you mean…?” both work out the edit distance from what you typed to each candidate word and pick the closest.
Picking whatever looks best right now at every step is called greedy, like packing a backpack “most valuable first” or “best value per kilo first”.

Greedy is quick and simple, but it does not always give the best result: the step that looks best now can block a better combination later. Dynamic programming compares every possibility in its table, so nothing is missed.

A backpack has a weight limit, every item has a weight and a value, and each item can be taken at most once: how do you pack the most value? This is the 0/1 knapsack: each item is taken 0 times or 1 time.

In the knapsack table the rows are items and the columns are capacities: a cell holds “the most value you can pack choosing only from the first few items, with this much room”. Look only at the last item, and it has just two fates: taken, or left.
Choosing courses, setting a budget, loading a container, handing out jobs to servers: it is behind all of them.

title.en: Rolling arrays and the unbounded knapsack

body.en: If each row only uses the row above it, there is no need to keep the whole table: keep a single row and rewrite it in place. This is a <part-ref to="roll"></part-ref>, and it can squash a table of thousands of rows into one.

Rewriting in place has a catch: the cell you read while rewriting another may already have been rewritten in this pass, and then it holds a value where this item has already been taken. The direction you rewrite in decides whether you read the old value or the new one.
A backpack where each item can be taken many times is the unbounded knapsack. The same circuit board, with only the rewrite direction changed, switches between the two kinds.

A cell need not hold a number; it can hold “yes / no” and answer “can it be done?” questions. Games where two players take turns fill a table this way too: each cell is a position, holding “can the player whose turn it is win?”.

Once you move, your opponent faces the new position. So whether a position wins depends on which positions you can send your opponent into. A position the player to move can always win is a winning position; one where every move loses is a losing position.
In some tables a cell has a fixed few ways in; in other problems the ways in are a whole run of earlier cells, and how many depends on the data.
The simplest example is the prefix sum: how much there is in all from the start up to here.
As long as the ways in are all earlier and already computed, the table can be filled however many there are and however they vary.
From a row of numbers, pick some from left to right, each bigger than the last, skipping any you like: how many can you pick? This is the longest increasing subsequence.

The key is the state: each cell holds the answer “ending with this one”, and the answer for the whole row is the largest of them. How many days in a run of share prices can be picked, each higher than the one before, is the same problem.
Making up an amount from coins of a few values, what is the fewest number of coins? And how many ways are there to pay? Cell i holds the answer for i.
Look only at the last coin: it could be any of the values, so the ways in are “one coin of each kind taken back”. The same table answers both “the fewest coins” and “how many ways to pay”.
The table only records how much has been made up, not which coins were used, so the ways it counts treat a different order of paying as a different way.
Can a string of letters with no spaces be split into words from a dictionary? Cell i holds “can the first i letters be split?”, as a “yes / no”.

Look only at the last word: it starts at some earlier position and ends here. A search engine facing a web address with no spaces, or a keyboard app facing a long run of pinyin, has to split it like this first.

In some problems the subproblems are stretches of the original string: from item i to item j. Lay them out as an interval table, where cell (i, j) holds that stretch’s answer; only half the table is used, since a stretch always starts before it ends.
Every stretch is worked out from shorter stretches: drop one end, or drop both. So as long as shorter stretches are done first, the table can be filled.
The longest palindromic subsequence and the best order to multiply a chain of matrices: they are both interval tables.
On a map with rewards and penalties, ask “how good is it to stand on each cell?”. A cell’s value depends on how good the neighbours it can reach are, with a discount for every step further away.

A rule like “value = the best result one step away, discounted” is called the Bellman equation. Start with every cell at 0 and scan round after round until nothing changes, and you have every cell’s value: this is value iteration.
It is one of the oldest foundations of reinforcement learning: game-playing programs and robots learning to walk all have to learn to judge “how good is it to be here?”.
Once the values are known, choosing a move is easy: always step to the neighbour with the highest value. Taken together, “what to do here” for every cell is called a policy.
Each cell looks only at its own neighbours, yet together they make a complete map for finding the way. Judge the values first, then follow them, and the policy grows by itself.

When the outcome is uncertain, an action’s value is the sum of its possible outcomes, each weighted by how likely it is; this is the . With an 80% chance of going right and 20% of going down, say, it is 0.8 × right + 0.2 × down.

Problems where every decision is made under uncertainty are called Markov decision processes, the mathematical skeleton of reinforcement learning. The rule is the familiar one: work out each action’s expectation, pick the best, discount it, and scan until it settles.

Which part of speech is each word in a sentence? Put the words in columns and the parts of speech in rows; each cell holds “the cheapest explanation so far, with the earlier words tagged and this word tagged this way”.
Each column only looks at the one before it. The best cell in the last column is the best tagging of the whole sentence, and backtracking reads off each word’s tag. This is the Viterbi algorithm.
Speech recognition turning sound into words, and keyboard apps turning pinyin into characters, use tables like this: one column per moment, one row per possibility.
Viterbi only wants the single best explanation. To count in every explanation and ask how likely the sentence is altogether, use the forward algorithm.
The shape of the table and every cell’s ways in are the same as in Viterbi; only a few components change. The same skeleton answers yet another question.
The same string of words means different things depending on how it is merged, two at a time, into phrases. Draw the merging and you get a parse tree.

How many ways a string of words can be merged is worked out in an interval table again: the last merge joins a left part and a right part at some split point. These counts are the Catalan numbers, which shoot up as the words grow in number.
Real parsing uses the CKY algorithm (also written CYK), which also checks grammar rules: which two parts can merge, and into what. The table has exactly the same shape.

Two long stretches of DNA may not be alike overall, yet hide a short piece that is very alike. Comparing from end to end is global alignment (the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm); looking only for the most alike piece is local alignment (the Smith-Waterman algorithm).
The key step in local alignment: once a score drops below 0 it is cut to 0, starting afresh from there. So the most alike piece can be anywhere in the table, and the answer is the largest cell in it.
Biologists searching gene databases for similar pieces use exactly this.
To make a picture narrower without squashing what is in it, find a seam running from top to bottom, one pixel per row, and cut it out.

Every pixel has an energy: the more it differs from its neighbours, the higher it is, as on the edges of letters. The seam with the least energy is a cheapest route, found the same way as any cheapest route, only heading in a different direction.
Cut one seam, work it out again, cut the next: this is content-aware resizing. Photo editors use it to turn a wide photo into a tall one.
